newsitem.title: UK: Watchdog clears UK of Indonesia arms-for-aid link.
newsitem.headline: Watchdog clears UK of Indonesia arms-for-aid link.

text.p: An official watchdog body cleared the British government on Thursday of linking aid projects in Indonesia to arms sales.
But the report by the National Audit Office (NAO) said proper performance targets were not set for some of the projects and at least one represented poor value for money.
The NAO began its study of seven projects in Indonesia with a total value of 46.4 million pounds ($78 million) after public concern there were links between the aid and arms sales.
There was also public concern that some of the aid covered activities in East Timor, an area annexed by Indonesia in 1975 in an act not recognised by the United Nations.

But the NAO said: "None of the projects examined included the procurement of military equipment... None of the contracts... were conditional on the Indonesian purchase of British goods and services beyond those necessary for the projects."
It also found that, with the exception of one project costing 8,000 pounds ($13,000), none were undertaken solely in East Timor.
But it said project appraisals for the Ombilin coal mine and another for radio studio rehabilitation had been rushed.

The radio studio project provided Radio Republik with what the NAO called "a superb broadcasting facility". But after 18 months, whole floors were unused or only partly used, although the situation has improved in the last year.
Some equipment supplied for the mine was inappropriate, much of it was unused and in 1995 it was transferred to another coal face when the Ombilin mine ceased to be financially sustainable.
The NAO called for better assessment of projects, both before and after completion, to ensure they met objectives.
It also called for all aid projects to be assessed to ensure they met development criteria.
The report was in part prompted by a 1994 court ruling that the government acted unlawfully in authorising 234 million pounds in aid for the Pergau dam project in Malaysia.
The government admitted the aid became "entangled" with a one billion pound sale of British arms to Malaysia in 1988.

The then foreign secretary Douglas Hurd ordered Britain's overseas aid agency to tighten up its procedures and decided to fund three more projects, including one in Indonesia, outside the aid budget to avoid problems in the light of the ruling.

The Pergau affair deeply embarrassed the British government and sparked a trade row with Malaysia, which objected to British media coverage of the issue and banned British firms from government contracts. The ban was lifted after seven months.
